title: "Master!"
hookLine: Zuigan calls to himself each day, "Master!" and answers "Yes!" (Gateless Gate 12)

cards: Somewhere in a monastery in old China, a monk calls out: Master! There's no one else he's calling. He answers himself: Yes!
Then he goes on. Wake up! Yes!
From now on, don't be fooled by anyone. Yes! Yes!
The Gateless Gate says he did this every day. Zen keeps the story as case twelve: the monk who called his own name.

teach.b: First, the man: Ruiyan, Zuigan in Japanese. The case gives one picture of him, a daily habit of calling out to himself and answering. Master here isn't a teacher across the room.
It's the one inside, the one he's trying to rouse. Second, the three calls. The first is just a name: are you there?
The second, wake up: be here, not half asleep in your own life.
The third, don't be fooled by others, any day, any time. That could mean other people's opinions, or the stories the mind tells about itself. The case doesn't explain; he just answers, yes, yes.
Wumen, the compiler, isn't simply impressed.

In paraphrase, he says old Ruiyan buys and sells himself, putting on a whole set of masks: one to call, one to answer, one awake, one that won't be fooled. Take any mask as the real thing, and you've missed it.
Copy Ruiyan, Wumen says, and your understanding is like a fox's. So this isn't a tidy self-help trick; its own collector pokes at it. Fourth, why it stays.
For long stretches of a day, attention runs on its own, like a car with nobody checking the road. Calling your own name taps the shoulder.
Some readers hear Ruiyan's practice as kind: he doesn't scold himself, he just calls and answers yes. And the koan leaves the question underneath wide open: who is it that answers?

how: Zen students may be given this case as a koan; some also take Ruiyan's habit as a simple reminder, pausing during the day to call themselves back to attention.

o: a student's call to summon his teacher
a polite word monks use to greet a guest
a monk's daily call to wake himself up

s: Ruiyan was calling to his teacher in the next room
he was calling to himself and answering himself.
Wumen's comment simply praises Ruiyan's habit
Wumen says Ruiyan puts on masks, and warns against copying him.
the case says Ruiyan did this every day
it's a daily habit, not a single moment.

games.q: you're Wumen, gathering this case into your collection. how do you comment on the monk who calls his own name each day?
o: praise it as the perfect method to copy.
tease him for wearing masks, and warn against imitation.
leave it with no comment at all.
games.why: Wumen says Ruiyan buys and sells himself with a set of masks, and that copying him gives a fox's understanding. even a practice worth keeping can turn into a role.

practice: Silently call your own name, warm and plain, the way a friend would from across a kitchen, then answer: yes. Notice the half second after the call, a small waking up, a coming back to the room, and rest in it.
When you drift, call again just as kindly, with no scolding, only the call and the yes.

wordCard.voice: Master! Ruiyan's daily call to himself in case twelve of the Gateless Gate, with his own answer, yes: wake up, and don't be fooled. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: the word Ruiyan calls out, often rendered 'master' or 'master of the house'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up. Who it is that answers is still the open question. Go gently.
